core_concepts: Welcome to the art of being human
The other day I was out for coffee with my friend Dave
I live in Portland, which is basically the best city for coffee in the world
All of which leads me to Dave
Dave had asked if we could get together and talk about his fight with depression
Dave wasn’t suicidal or anything, just unhappy
My take on depression is that it’s more of a symptom than a disease
Dave was kind enough to put up with my interrogation — Are you sleeping enough?
Then I started asking questions about his job
Do you like what you do?
It’s a good job, he said
Yes, but do you like what you do?
mechanisms_or_explanations: Dave had asked if we could get together and talk about his fight with depression
A better man because of it, oddly enough
I mean, if you wanted a great deal on a commercial fluorescent, he was your man
So I asked Dave one of my favorite questions, If you could do anything, what would you do?
How could something as mundane and ordinary as a job change everything for Dave?
I would argue it’s because what we do is central to our humanness
What’s the first question we usually ask somebody when we meet them?
When you wake up every morning, what is it you do with your small ration of oxygen?
The moments when we wish life had a Pause button
In the church, we often spend the majority of our time teaching people how to live the minority of their lives
I teach people how to read the Scriptures and pray and do God stuff
critical_qualifiers: My own tangle with depression was brutal and terrifying, but I made it through, and here I am
I learned a fair bit through my years in the maw of the beast, and I’m always happy to help however I can
But he had no clue why
So usually with somebody like Dave I start digging
But he couldn’t think of anything “wrong” with him
Yes, but do you like what you do?
He can hold his breath under water for like three days
What about the fact that even here in the US, unless you come from money, it’s incredibly hard just to eke out a living?
